lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Order these draft moves: write the resolution; list the complication; sketch who/where.

FEEDBACK
Sketch who/where → list complication → write resolution (after attempts).

CHECK
Polishing commas in paragraph one before the plot exists wastes drafting energy.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Draft a 220–280 word narrative with clear orientation, complication, two attempts and a resolution. Use paragraph breaks at time/place shifts. Note two places you will revise later.

Write a short reflection describing one specific revision you made and why.
lesson.learning_intention: Drafting a longer narrative means planning orientation, complication, attempts and resolution across paragraphs before polishing every sentence.
lesson.offline_alternative: Use paper and pencil to complete the original task, then retain a photograph or short parent observation as evidence.
lesson.parent_notes:
Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: Draft a 220–280 word narrative with clear orientation, complication, two attempts and a resolution. Use paragraph breaks at time/place shifts. Note two places you will revise later. Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Written model 1: Original response on new material: Sketch who/where → list complication → write resolution (after attempts). Reasoning: I used draft by attending to narrative rather than copying the worked model.

Parent: Written model 2: Common error: Polishing commas in paragraph one before the plot exists wastes drafting energy. Correction: Sketch who/where → list complication → write resolution (after attempts). Why: the correction restores accurate use of draft.

Parent: Likely misconception: Polishing commas in paragraph one before the plot exists wastes drafting energy. Keep sample answers out of the child role.

Parent: Short-answer focus 1: Produce a fresh example demonstrating draft on new material (not the worked model). Explain the particular words, sources or choices that make it work.

Parent: Short-answer focus 2: Name one likely error with draft, correct it, and explain why the correction helps a reader or audience.

Parent: Marking notes: Require independently produced work with a specific supporting detail. / Require misconception + correction + purpose-linked reason..

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
Plan: Ori — Sam at the ferry; Comp — ticket missing; Attempts — search bag, ask attendant; Res — ticket in the book used as a fan. Draft paragraphs follow that mountain, leaving spelling fixes for later.

TRY FIRST
Order these draft moves: write the resolution; list the complication; sketch who/where.

FEEDBACK
Sketch who/where → list complication → write resolution (after attempts).
teach_steps.explain:
Drafting a longer narrative means planning orientation, complication, attempts and resolution across paragraphs before polishing every sentence.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner make decisions based on specific language evidence, rather than guess or copy someone else. Keep the meaning accurate and explain the choice.

HOW TO WORK
Read the original example and locate the words or actions that support the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Check your response against the feedback: did you address the same skill and show your reasoning? If a detail is uncertain, identify what would have to be checked. One deliberate, justified revision is more useful than making the answer longer.
